To: Engineering leadership
From: Platform team
Re: Buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

Recommendation: do not approve a broad hardware purchase yet. Fund a focused utilisation and scheduling effort first, with a narrowly scoped purchase only for proven, persistent bottlenecks. If the next two quarters show sustained demand above roughly 70 percent average utilisation with healthy tail latency, then revisit procurement with a specific model, quantity, and lease or refresh plan.

The tempting option is to buy more GPUs and treat capacity as the answer. That is understandable, but it risks confusing scarcity with waste. Our current estate is not simply too small; it is too unevenly used. Some workloads are interactive and latency-sensitive, while others are batch-like and tolerate queuing. Some models are large but rarely used, while smaller models are hammered by many services. Without better visibility, a purchase would likely add idle capacity, not speed.

Cost is the first constraint, but it is not only the sticker price. Local hardware carries capital outlay, power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, and the opportunity cost of engineers spending time on provisioning instead of product work. Cloud or rented capacity shifts some of that into variable spend, but it introduces network dependence, data-residency questions, and less predictable latency. The right comparison is not “owned versus rented” in the abstract; it is total cost per useful inference, including idle time, failures, and the delay to ship.

Latency matters differently by workload. A user-facing assistant needs tight p95 and p99 behaviour, not just average throughput. A nightly evaluation job can wait. If we buy more hardware without separating these classes, we may improve average utilisation while making interactive requests worse through queuing. Better scheduling, admission control, priority lanes, and model routing can often recover more user-visible performance than additional accelerators.

Reliability is also underweighted. More devices can mean more failure modes: driver drift, thermal events, degraded nodes, network partitions, and operational toil. A small number of well-monitored, well-tested machines may be more dependable than a larger fleet that nobody fully understands. We should track not only throughput but also error rate, restart frequency, queue depth, and time-to-recover. If a node fails, the system should degrade gracefully rather than stall a critical path.

Opportunity cost deserves explicit attention. Every week spent tuning utilisation is a week not spent on features, evaluation, or safety work. That is a real cost, but it is bounded and reversible. A large purchase is harder to reverse: once racks are installed and contracts signed, the organisation becomes committed to a capacity level that may not match demand. Reversibility favors staged action: instrument first, pilot second, buy third.

Uncertainty is substantial. Model sizes are moving quickly, inference demand may grow faster than expected, and pricing for both local and rented capacity can shift. We do not know whether the next model generation will be cheaper to serve or more demanding. We also do not know whether our current bottleneck is compute, memory, data movement, or simply poor routing. The honest position is that we can reduce risk now, but we cannot know the final capacity requirement with confidence.

The practical path is a 90-day programme. Instrument every service with request class, model, queue time, inference time, cache hit rate, and failure mode. Separate interactive from batch traffic. Add admission control and priority scheduling. Evaluate quantization, distillation, caching, and smaller specialist models where quality permits. Review whether some workloads should move to managed inference or be redesigned to need fewer tokens. Then set a decision gate: if sustained utilisation remains low, the purchase case is weak; if utilisation is high and latency is poor, the case is strong.

I would also ask for a small, reversible purchase only if a specific bottleneck is proven, such as a latency-critical model that cannot meet p95 targets without dedicated capacity. Prefer leases or short-term commitments over permanent ownership where possible. Keep a clear exit plan: refresh cycle, resale or redeployment path, and a rule that unused capacity is reviewed quarterly.

In short, the best next step is not more hardware; it is better evidence and better use of the hardware we already have. Buy only when the data says the constraint is real, persistent, and not fixable through routing, scheduling, or model design. That approach is slower than a blanket purchase, but it is cheaper, more reversible, and more likely to improve the experience users actually feel.

Internal engineering memo: buy more local AI hardware, or use what we have better?

Recommendation up front: do not make a broad hardware purchase yet. Spend the next two quarters improving utilisation, scheduling, observability, and workload shaping on the systems we already own. Buy additional capacity only where the evidence shows a durable, latency-sensitive bottleneck that software cannot remove. That is not a blanket refusal to spend; it is a discipline of buying after the bottleneck is named.

The current position is that demand is rising faster than our ability to explain where time is going. Some workloads are bursty and tolerate queuing. Others, especially interactive inference and evaluation loops, are sensitive to tail latency. The same GPU pool is being asked to serve experiments, batch scoring, fine-tuning, and internal tools. That mix makes utilisation look deceptively healthy while individual requests still wait. A new box would add peak capacity, but it would not fix poor batching, idle memory, duplicated models, or jobs that hold resources longer than they need.

Cost is the first constraint, but it is not simply the sticker price. Local hardware has capital cost, power, cooling, maintenance, spare parts, and staff time. Cloud or rented capacity has variable cost and can be easier to scale, but it may introduce network latency, data-residency questions, and less predictable billing. The right comparison is not “owned versus rented” in the abstract; it is cost per useful request at the latency we actually need. If a workload can be moved to a cheaper tier, cached, distilled, or run less often, the savings may exceed the cost of a new node. If a workload is genuinely latency-critical and cannot be batched, then hardware may be the only honest fix.

Latency deserves separate treatment from throughput. A team can be “underused” on average while still failing users because p95 or p99 latency is bad. We should instrument queue time, model load time, token generation time, cache hit rate, and retry rate before buying. If most delay is queueing, better scheduling and admission control will help. If most delay is model load or memory pressure, a larger or better-placed machine may help. If most delay is network or storage, neither local GPUs nor more GPUs will help much.

Reliability is the second reason to be cautious. More hardware increases the number of failure modes: drivers, firmware, thermal events, power interruptions, and human configuration drift. A small team cannot operate a large fleet well. Reliability improves when workloads are simpler, health checks are clearer, and capacity is sized with headroom rather than pushed to the edge. Buying hardware to chase average utilisation can reduce headroom and make incidents worse.

Opportunity cost matters as much as direct spend. Every dollar and every engineer-week spent on hardware is a dollar and week not spent on evaluation, data quality, model selection, or product features. The team’s scarcest resource is attention. If the bottleneck is unclear, buying hardware is a way to avoid the harder work of measurement. That is tempting, but it is usually the wrong trade.

Reversibility also favors the software-first path. Scheduling changes, caching, autoscaling, and workload isolation are reversible. A new rack is not. If we buy too much and the workload mix changes, we own idle capacity. If we improve utilisation and still hit a hard limit, we can buy with confidence and a clear business case.

Uncertainty is real. Demand may grow faster than expected. Some models may require more memory than we can fit. Latency requirements may tighten. We should not pretend the current data is complete. The plan should include a short measurement window, a decision gate, and a pre-agreed trigger for purchase. For example, if after two quarters of improved scheduling the p95 latency remains above target, or if a proven workload cannot fit in memory, then purchase should be approved. If utilisation improves and latency stabilises, the hardware case weakens.

The practical path is to instrument first, then tune. Separate interactive from batch workloads. Add admission control so interactive requests are not starved by bulk jobs. Cache model loads and common outputs. Reduce duplicate deployments. Track cost per request and latency by workload, not only by machine. Keep a small reserve of capacity for spikes rather than running at the edge.

So the recommendation is: improve utilisation now, buy selectively later. Do not let the desire for more hardware substitute for evidence. If the evidence later shows a durable shortfall, the purchase will be easier to defend, easier to size, and less likely to strand capacity. If the evidence shows that the problem is operational, the savings will be immediate and the team will be better prepared for the next wave of demand.
